title: The Price of the Last Chair

beats.text: In nineteen oh one, a railroad stock went up ten times in one week.
You borrowed shares, sold them, and plan to buy back cheaper.
But two railroad giants want the same company.
Harriman buys in secret. Hill and Morgan's bank buy to stop him.
So why is that your problem?
You see, it's like selling a neighbor's ladder, then finding someone bought every ladder in town.
On May ninth, every short seller needs shares at once.
Musical chairs, and the music stopped.
Short sellers dump everything else to pay, and the market crashes.
The giants call a truce and let them off the hook.
And the railroad? Exactly the same.
That thousand dollars wasn't a railroad's price. It was the price of the last chair.

facts.claim: May 1901: Northern Pacific common went to about ten times its price of a week earlier (under/about $100 to $1,000)
Peak of $1,000 a share came on Thursday, May 9, 1901
E. H. Harriman (Union Pacific, with Kuhn, Loeb) bought Northern Pacific quietly to take control; James J. Hill and J.P. Morgan's bank bought to keep it (fight began over the Burlington railroad)
Most of the shares sold in the frenzy had been sold short; more shares were sold short than could be bought back
Short sellers sold other stocks to cover, and the broader market crashed (Panic of 1901)
The Morgan and Kuhn, Loeb groups called a truce and did not force delivery from the short sellers

caption:
May 1901: Northern Pacific went from about $100 to $1,000 a share in a week.
Harriman on one side, Hill and Morgan's bank on the other, short sellers caught in the middle, and the rest of the market crashed.
Same trains. Same tracks.
